full_judgment:
This Rule obtained under the former section 115(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure arises out of a probate proceeding. The petitioner filed Miscellaneous Case No.8 of 1976 (probate) in the Court of the District Delegate and Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Faridpur for grant of probate. The case was taken up for ex parte disposal on 28.11.78 after issuance of notices by the District Delegate under Section 283 of the Succession Act calling upon all persons claiming to have any interest in the estate of the deceased to come and see the proceedings before the grant of probate. On the day of disposal ex parte the Assistant Custodian, Enemy Property entered appearance and claimed that the will in question was a forged one and that he would resist the claim. The application was filed under Order 1, Rule 10 C.P.C. for being added as a party to the probate proceeding. 

 3. The Assistant Custodian, Enemy Property instituted Civil Revision No. 5 of 1980 in the Court of the District Judge, Faridpur under the former section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure against the aforesaid judgment and order of the District Delete. The learned District Judge, Faridpur by his Judgment and order dated 2.5.83 allowed the civil revisional case and set aside the order of the District Delegateon the ground that when the Assistant Custodian entered appearance and objected to the proceedingsthere was a "contention" within the meaning of Section 286 of the Succession Act and therefore the District Delegate should have referred the matter to the learned District Judge for adjudication. The grant Of probate under such circumstances was completely without jurisdiction. Thereafter the petitioner obtained the present Rule. 

 4. It has been submitted that the civil revision case before the District Judge, Faridpur was incompetent because at the time when the revisional application was preferred, the District Judge had pecuniary jurisdiction to entertain an appeal only up to a valuation of Tk. 20,000/- under section 21 (1) of the Civil Courts Act. The case of Nurul Islam vs. Abdur Rashid, 32 DLR 259 has been cited for the proposition that the District Judge's revisional jurisdiction under the former section 115(2) C.P.C. was restricted by his appellate jurisdiction as provided under section 21(1) of the Civil Courts Act. In other words, the District Judge could exercise revisional jurisdiction under the former section 115(2) only in respect of those cases where the value of the subject-matter did not exceed Tk. 20,000/-. In all other cases, it was the High Court Division which exercised jurisdiction under the former section 115(1). 

 5. The learned District Judge has pronounced his judgment and order on 2.5.83. By the Civil Courts (Amendment) Ordinance 1983 (Ordinance No. II of 1983), the appellate jurisdiction of the District Judge was enhanced to a valuation of Tk. 70,000/- with effect from the coming into force of the said Ordinance, i.e from 16.1.83. The present probate proceeding was valued at Tk. 45,000/-. Therefore on the date of disposal of the civil revisional case the District Judge was quite competent to entertain the revisional application. The first contention of the petitioner, therefore fails. 

 It has next been contended that there was no "contention" before the District Delegate by mere filing of an application for being added as a party, because in any view of the matter the Assistant Custodian, Enemy Property had no interest in the estate of the deceased. Mr. Kazi Ebadul Huq, learned Advocate for the petitioner, has cited the case of Sreemati Charubala Sen Gupta vs. Abul Hashem and others (1981) 33 DLR (AD) 254= 1981 BLD (AD) 218'= and has submitted that in a proceeding for the probate of a will what the Court is required to see is whether the will was duly executed and if there is evidence to that effect the Court will grant the probate. It is not the concern of the probate Court whether the testator had title to the property or whether he had any authority to otherwise deal with the property. He further submits that the Assistant Custodian has claimed an interest outside or independently of the will. He has no interest in the estate through the testator. Therefore he has no locus standi to be added as party to the probate proceeding. The District Delegate was, therefore, quite justified in rejecting his application for being added as a party. 

 6. The afforested case [(1961) 33 DLR(AD) 254] was decided on a construction of section 283(1) of the Succession Act. The Appellate Division decided that the Enemy property authority could not come through the testator and therefore it cannot come and see the proceedings before grant of probate. It was a proceeding before a District Judge, not a District Delegate. The Appellate Division left the question unanswered as to whether the provisions of Order 1, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure are applicable to a probate proceeding or not. In the present case the opposite party filed its application under Order 1, rule 10 C.P.C. and the present proceedings were before a District Delegate, not a District Judge and therefore it cannot be said that the aforecited case applies on all fours in present case. 

 8. I am clearly of the opinion that the proceedings of the District Judge and the District Delegate in respect of grant of probate and Letters of Administration are not the same. Section 265 of the Succession Act provides that the High Court may appoint such judicial officers within any District as it thinks fit to act for the District Judge as Delegates to grant probate and Letters of Administration "in non contentious cases". Persons so appointed shall be called "District Delegates." Section 272 of the Succession Act provides that the District Delegate may grant probate and Letters of Administration "in any case in which there is no contention." Section 286 of the Succession Act is prohibitory in nature and forbids a District Delegate to grant probate or Letters of Administration "in any case in which there is contention as to the grant." In the Explanation to section 286 it has been provided that "contention" means the appearance of anyone in person or by his recognised agent or by a pleader duly appointed to act on his behalf, to oppose the proceeding." 

 9. When an application for grant of probate or Letter of Administration is filed both the District Judge and the District Delegate may, under section 283, if they think proper, issue citations calling upon all persons claiming to have any interest in the estate of the deceased to come and see the proceedings before the grant of probate and Letters of Administration. But it is only the District Judge who can dispose of an objector's application, when he appears in response to the citations. Section 268 of the Succession Act provides that such proceedings before the District Judge, save as otherwise provided in the Succession Act, shall be regulated, so far as the circumstances of the case permit, by the Code of Civil Procedure. The proceedings before the District Delegate are not so regulated. In his Court, whenever anyone appears in person, or by his recognised agent, or by a pleader duly appointed to act on his behalf, to oppose the proceeding, the District Delegate has to stop the proceeding. The proceeding before him ceases to be non-contentious. And he can only deal with non-contentious cases. Section 288 of the Succession Act provides, inter alia, that in every case in which there is contention, the petition and documents shall be returned to the applicant for presentation to the District Judge. Alternatively the District Delegate is authorised to impound the same for the purposes of justice and shall send the same to the District Judge. 

 10. When there is an appearance, therefore, the proceeding before the District Delegate ceased to be non-contentious and if the District Delegate proceeds with the case he will exceed his jurisdiction. It is not for him to decide about the merit of the contention." He is not to take a decision whether the application under Order 1, rule 10 C.P.C. ought to be allowed or not. Once an appearance takes pace under section 286(1) he becomes functus officio. The District Delegate has no other option but to close the proceeding and to send the same to the District Judge or return the same to the petitioner for presentation to the proper Court under section 288 of the Succession Act. Whether the party opposing the proceeding has any locus standi or not will be decided not by him but by the District Judge and this revisional Court is also not expressing any opinion in the matter. Sections 265, 272 and 286 of the Succession Act make it quite clear that the District Delegate's power to grant a probate or Letter of Administration is strictly confined to non-contentious cases and the definition of "contention" being what it is he has no jurisdiction to decide whether the contention is well-taken or not.
